content: 1. Vogel JP, Souza JP, and Gülmezoglu AM conducted a secondary analysis of the WHO Global Survey on Maternal and Neonatal Health to examine patterns and outcomes of labor induction in Africa and Asia. Their findings were published in PLoS One in 2013 (Volume 8, Issue 6, Article e65612). 2. Guerra GV, Cecatti JG, Souza JP, Faúndes A, Morais SS, Gülmezoglu AM, and colleagues compared elective induction of labor with spontaneous labor in Latin America. Their study was published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in September 2011 (Volume 89, Issue 9, Pages 657–665). 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) released recommendations on labor induction in 2011, providing evidence-based guidance for clinical practice. These recommendations are available through the WHO's Geneva office. 4. The WHO Executive Guideline Steering Group for Updating Maternal and Perinatal Health Recommendations (2017–2019) developed updated guidelines, accessible via the WHO reproductive health publications website as of December 7, 2018. 5. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (Second Edition) was published in 2014, offering a comprehensive framework for creating evidence-based health guidelines. 6. Middleton P, Shepherd E, and Crowther CA reviewed the induction of labor for improving birth outcomes in women at or beyond term. Their systematic review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2018 (Issue 5, Article CD004945). 7. Balshem H, Helfand M, Schünemann HJ, Oxman AD, Kunz R, Brozek J, and colleagues outlined the GRADE guidelines for rating the quality of evidence. Their work was published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2011 (Volume 64, Issue 4, Pages 401–406). 8. Downe S, Finlayson K, Tunçalp Ö, and Metin Gülmezoglu A conducted a systematic scoping review to identify processes and outcomes of antenatal care that are important to healthy pregnant women. Their findings were published in BJOG in 2016 (Volume 123, Issue 4, Pages 529–539). 9. Downe S, Finlayson K, Oladapo O, Bonet M, and Gülmezoglu A performed a systematic qualitative review to determine what matters to women during childbirth. Their study was published in PLoS One in 2018 (Volume 13, Issue 4, Article e0194906). 10. Mazzoni A, Althabe F, Liu NH, Bonotti AM, Gibbons L, Sánchez AJ, and colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies to assess women's preferences for cesarean section. Their findings were published in BJOG in 2011 (Volume 118, Issue 4, Pages 391–399). 11. Kaimal AJ, Little SE, Odibo AO, Stamilio DM, Grobman WA, Long EF, and colleagues evaluated the cost-effectiveness of elective labor induction at 41 weeks in nulliparous women. Their study was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 12. Hannah ME, Hannah WJ, Hellmann J, Hewson S, Milner R, and Willan A compared labor induction with serial antenatal monitoring in post-term pregnancy in a randomized controlled trial. This study, conducted by the Canadian Multicenter Post-term Pregnancy Trial Group, was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1992 (Volume 326, Issue 24, Pages 1587–1592). 13. Goeree R, Hannah M, and Hewson S analyzed the cost-effectiveness of labor induction versus serial antenatal monitoring in the Canadian Multicenter Post-term Pregnancy Trial. Their findings were published in CMAJ in 1995 (Volume 152, Issue 9, Pages 1445–1450). 14. Alfirevic Z, Keeney E, Dowswell T, Welton NJ, Medley N, Dias S, and colleagues conducted a systematic review, network meta-analysis, and cost-effectiveness analysis to determine the best method for labor induction. Their work was published in Health Technology Assessment in 2016 (Volume 20, Issue 65, Pages 1–584). 15. The WHO published the State of Inequality: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health report in 2015, addressing disparities in health outcomes and care. 16. Heimstad R, Romundstad PR, Hyett J, Mattsson LA, and Salvesen KA explored women's experiences and attitudes toward expectant management and labor induction for post-term pregnancy. Their study was published in Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica in 2007 (Volume 86, Issue 8, Pages 950–956). 17. Martin D, Thompson W, Pinkerton J, and Watson J conducted a randomized controlled trial on selective planned delivery. Their findings were published in the British Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in 1978. 18. Roberts LJ and Young KR analyzed women's attitudes toward the management of prolonged pregnancy before and after term. Their study was published in the British Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in 1991 (Volume 98, Issue 11, Pages 1102–1106). 19. Gatward H, Simpson M, Woodhart L, and Stainton MC examined women's experiences of being induced for post-date pregnancy. Their study was published in Women and Birth in 2010 (Volume 23, Issue 1, Pages 3–9). 20. Vogel JP, Gülmezoglu AM, Hofmeyr GJ, and Temmerman M provided a global perspective on elective labor induction. Their work was published in Clinical Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2014 (Volume 57, Issue 2, Pages 331–342). 21. The WHO released recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience in 2016, emphasizing evidence-based practices to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. 22. The WHO published standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities in 2016, providing a framework for enhancing care delivery. 23. The WHO's guideline development group and external experts contributed to the preparation of recommendations on labor induction at or beyond term, ensuring evidence-based and contextually relevant guidance.
